Row 11 (n=37): "I would like my avatar to be a man character, so please set it and keep it for later instead of resetting it."
SOP: k1 coordination conjunction "so" conjunction "and" conjunct c1, c3, c4. c1 declarative; c3 imperative set; c4 imperative keep; r3 instead of → c5 nonfinite resetting.
Coordination joining declarative c1 with imperatives — is that allowed? The rules: "A command or a question cannot stand inside another clause, so a coordination that joins an imperative or interrogative clause with such a clause [a clause that ends a relation with a marker] has a wrong conjunct: L3."

Here, the coordination joins c1 (declarative, main clause "I would like..."), c3 and c4 (imperatives). Is a coordination of a declarative with imperatives wrong? The prohibition was for clauses inside a relation. "so" here: "so please set it" — "so" as conjunction joining the clause. This is a "so" that connects two sentences/clauses; the schema options: relation marked "so" or coordination. Both accepted per the settled case about "and after that". Here coordination with declarative + imperative conjuncts: is a command able to be a conjunct of a coordination with a declarative? Nothing forbids it explicitly. The rule about imperative conjunct only covers clauses ending a relation with a marker. I'd accept. But wait: is c5 "resetting it" inside relation r3 from c4 → c5; c5 is a nonfinite clause, fine (not imperative/interrogative).

Hmm, but there's a subtlety: r3 from c4 to c5 "instead of resetting it". Fine.

L8 for row 11? Let me check "keep it for later" — n6 "later" head of nominal, relation "for". Fine. "please" in discourse of c3 — fine.

One concern: "set it" and "keep it" complements "it" — fine.

L8.

Row 12 (n=38): "Make my avatar the male figure; that is the figure I want every time I open the app or start a new drawing."
SOP: c1 imperative Make complement n1 n2; n3 "that"; c2 declarative is subject n3 complement n4; n5 I; c3 declarative want subject n5 complement n6 ("every time")?? Hmm "want every time I open..." — c3 verb want subject n5 complement n6 "every time"; c4 declarative open subject n7 complement n8; k1 coordination "or" c4 c5 (start); c5 declarative start complement n9; k2 coordination c1 c2; r1 from n4 to c3; r2 from n6 to k1.

Issues: "want" is given complement n6 "every time" and "every time I open the app or start a new drawing" — the figure wanted. Hmm, "the figure I want every time I open the app" — "want" takes "the figure" as object which is r1 from n4 to c3. c3's complement is n6 "every time" — that's a time adjunct treated as complement. Not judged (what a complement is to the verb is not judged). Fine.

k1 coordination "or" joining c4 and c5: c5 has no subject — sharing subject "I"? c5 declarative verb start, no subject. Per settled case, a verb after "and"/"then" following a clause with subject and auxiliary may share them. "open the app or start a new drawing" — no auxiliary, but sharing subject for "or" coordination is normal. Subject omission: is it L4 (subject the words do not show)? The words do show the shared subject through coordination. Acceptable? The settled case covers "and"/"then" with auxiliary. For "or" with present tense verbs, subject sharing is standard grammar. I'd accept.

k2 joins c1 and c2 without conjunction (semicolon). Fine.

Wait: "that is the figure I want" — "that" as subject nominal head. OK.

Hmm, one thing: c5 has no complement? "start a new drawing" - complement n9. ok.

L8 for row 12.

Row 13 (n=40): "I would like my avatar to stay a male figure no matter which diagram or drawing I open, so please remember it for the next session too."
SOP: c2 nonfinite stay modifier "no" modifier "matter" subject n2 complement n3; n4 "which diagram"; k1 "or" n4 n5; c3 declarative open subject n6 ("I") complement k1; k2 "so" c1 c4; r3 from c2 to c3.

"no matter which diagram" — held as modifiers "no" "matter" and then "which diagram or drawing I open" as a clause tied to c2 by r3. Plausible. "too" as modifier of c4. Fine.

Is anything wrong? c3 "open" has subject n6 and complement k1 (a coordination of nominals "which diagram or drawing"). Fine.

L8.

Row 14 (n=41): "Could you set my avatar to the man and keep that figure every time I start a new drawing, instead of asking me again?"
SOP: c1 interrogative aux Could verb set subject n1 complement n2; r1 to n3; k1 "and" conjunct c1, c2, c5; c2 interrogative verb keep (no subject — shared with c1's "you"); c5 fragment ellipsis=c2 — what is c5? "instead of asking me again" — hmm, c5 is a fragment with ellipsis to c2. And r2 "instead of" from c5 to c4 (nonfinite asking). c5 seems to represent an elided clause "instead of asking me again" that shares the verb "keep"? Hmm.

Actually the structure: "keep that figure every time I start a new drawing, instead of asking me again" — "instead of asking me again" is an adjunct of "keep". The sop writes c5 as a fragment with ellipsis=c2 (sharing "keep"), coordinated as a third conjunct, and then r2 from c5 to c4 (the nonfinite). That's inventing an elliptical clause "keep ... instead of asking me again"? That's odd: c5 is a fragment sharing the verb of c2 while having no words of its own except... wait every word must be in exactly one value. c5 has no words at all! A clause with no words. Is that a wrong statement (L4: a coordination between wires the message doesn't relate / ellipsis on a fragment that shares no verb)?

Hmm, c5 has form=fragment, ellipsis=c2, and no words. The judgement: "Whether a fragment shares the verb of another clause (ellipsis)" is #3 in what must be right. An empty fragment representing an elided repetition... Suspicious. The words "instead of asking me again" form c4 (nonfinite) with relation "instead of" from c5 to c4. But the start of the relation should be the clause c2 (keep) or a nominal of it — "the start of a relation with a marker: the clause, or any nominal of that clause". A start at an empty fragment clause c5 which itself is an ellipsis of c2... arguably it stands for the clause. But is an empty clause a wrong statement? It states that there's an elided clause which shares "keep". Hmm.

Is it L3 "A relation has ... a start the words rule out"? Starting at an empty fragment that refers to the same clause... I'd say borderline. Hmm.

Also, k1 joins c1, c2, c5 — c5 being an empty clause joined as third conjunct. That says "set my avatar to the man, and keep that figure, and (elided) instead of asking me again" — this is a coordination with conjunects where the third has no words.

Alternatively judge L8 (acceptable reading; the next layer can understand that "instead of asking me again" modifies an elided version of "keep"). It's not "undoing a wrong statement" — the empty fragment with ellipsis=c2 does carry the meaning that the adjunct belongs to "keep". Actually r2's from=c5=bogus, but c5 ≡ c2 semantically.

Hmm. I lean L8: the reading is recoverable, nothing lost, no wrong statement about words. But wait — is there any wrong statement? "keep that figure every time I start a new drawing" — n5 "every time" complement; r3 from n5 to c3. Fine. c2 has no subject: interrogative "Could you set ... and keep" shares "you". Per rules, sharing subject is allowed when clause has no subject and follows a question? The settled case is about declarative/imperative after "and". A second interrogative conjunct without subject is normal grammar ("Could you set it and keep it?"). Fine.

I'd give L8. Hmm, but the empty clause bugs me. Let me reconsider: "Words of one written clause are held in another" (L1). Not applicable. "A coordination has a wrong conjunct" (L3) — is c5 a wrong conjunct? It's a clause with no words at all; the message has nothing coordinated. That's a bit like "a relation or a coordination between wires that the message does not relate" (L4). Hmm.

Honestly, the intent of c5: the formalizer wanted to attach "instead of asking me again" as a relation, and needed a start; it couldn't start at c2 because... it could have. Creating an empty elliptical clause to host the relation is a formal device. I think a fair judge accepts — but it's arguably an invented clause (L4: "The circuit states what the message does not say"). The ellipsis case in L4 is "ellipsis on a fragment that shares no verb ('move the box, and thanks')". Here the empty fragment does share the verb of c2 — the claim is precisely that. So it's not that L4 case.

I'll accept L8. Given the instruction "Judge fairly: a plausible or incomplete reading that the next layer can continue from is acceptable".

Row 15 (n=45): "the male figure it is."
SOP: n1 "the male figure"; n2 "it"; c1 declarative verb is subject n2 complement n1. Fine, L8. (Reading: "the male figure it is" — "it is the male figure". Order not judged.)

Row 16 (n=46): "a man from now on."
SOP: n1 "a man"; r1 marker "from" from n1 to n2 ("now"); c1 fragment modifier "on" complement n1.
"a man from now on" — fixed phrase "from now on" split: relation from n1 (the nominal!) to "now", with "on" as clause modifier. Hmm: relation marked "from" starting at n1 "a man" — "The start of a relation with a marker: the clause, or any nominal of that clause that grammar allows". Does grammar allow "from" to start at "a man"? "a man from now on" — "from now on" modifies the whole; attaching "from now on" to "a man" modifies the nominal ("a man from now on") which is arguably acceptable — it describes the man from now on. Hmm, but "from now on" is a time phrase, and the settled case says "A word of time or order cannot describe a noun from where it stands" — that was about a word of time as a dependent of a nominal. Here "from now on" as a relation from the nominal... L3 says a relation with "a start the words rule out, such as a nominal of another clause". Starting at n1 (the only nominal) is grammatically not ruled out for "from" — "the man from now on"? Eh, weird but "from now" as a temporal prepositional phrase attaching to a nominal is odd.

Also, is "on" being a clause modifier wrong? It's a particle.

Hmm. Two sub-questions. This is one of those "several readings pass" gray zones. I think the safer judgement: the phrase "from now on" is a fixed time phrase; splitting it into a relation from the nominal plus "on" as a modifier of the fragment clause loses nothing explicit (all words present, all tied). There's no clause with a verb, so it's a fragment; complement n1; r1 from n1 (start at nominal — allowed by the "start of a relation" freedom) — pass. L8.

Wait, but is r1 tied? yes from n1 to n2. Nothing untied. L8.

OK. Let me continue reading. I need to be efficient. Let me do 6 rows per dump: 17-22.

But I also need to record verdicts. Let me start appending to /tmp/verdicts in batches after every few dumps. Actually I'll accumulate and write parts of the final file directly into the target path using bash heredoc appends (>> after first part with >). That's writing the file in a few large parts — allowed. But careful: if I append and later need to fix, I'd have to rewrite. Let me collect verdicts in /tmp/v1.jsonl etc., then concatenate at the end into the target. Safer.

Actually simplest: I'll keep the judgments in scratchpad notes after each group of ~20 rows (compact JSON lines). Then final assembly from scratchpad reads. Hmm, reading back costs tokens.

Best: append JSON lines to /tmp/part1.jsonl as I go with bash (cheap, one line per row, low tokens since I must type the content anyway). Then final: cat parts > target. Total typing = content once. Good.

Let me re-check row 5 (n=28) "Keep it as a male figure from here on." — sop has modifier "on" on c1 AND relation "from"→"here". "on" as a modifier of the clause is fine-ish. And in row 0 (n=10) "From now on, my avatar is a man figure." — @r1 marker "From" from c1 to n1 with "on" modifier on clause. Both pass per the "fixed phrase may be held whole as a modifier" freedom... but these don't hold it whole. Splitting a fixed phrase: "from now" as relation, "on" as clause modifier. I think this is acceptable; no wrong statement.

Hmm, wait. In row 0, is "on" a modifier of clause c1 which is "my avatar is a man figure"? A modifier holds "words that are neither nominals nor markers". "on" here is a preposition (linking word) without object... L3: "A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent" — is "on" a linking word here? In "from now on", "on" is not linking anything. It's part of an adverbial idiom. I'd not call it a linking word. Accept.

OK, continuing. But I'm worried about my leniency. The rule set gives L8 for "plausible or incomplete reading". Most formalizer outputs are careful. But with 150 rows and the design (sop vs alt), probably a mix of good and bad. Let me keep reading carefully for actual wrong statements.

Row 17 (n=50): "Change that to a man character, please." — fine, L8.

Row 18 (n=52): "Use a man for the avatar from now on." — sop like row 5, "on" modifier on clause, "from"→"now". L8.

Row 19 (n=53): "I changed my mind: a male figure."
SOP: c1 declarative changed; c2 fragment complement n3; k1 coordination (no conjunction) conjunct c1 c2. Fine — the colon creates a coordination or a relation. L8.

Row 20 (n=54): "Actually, set the avatar to the man and keep that instead of the one we just discussed."
SOP: c2 imperative keep complement=$k2 where k2 is a coordination with conjunction "instead of" joining n3 "that" and n4 "the one". Hmm. "keep that instead of the one we just discussed" — "instead of" is a prepositional marker; treating it as a conjunction of a coordination between two nominals. Is that acceptable? L3: "A coordination has a wrong conjunct" or "A linking word is held as a modifier or a dependent" — not exactly. "instead of" as a conjunction joining two nominals: "keep that instead of the one" — the coordination of "that" and "the one" as the thing kept; that asserts both are kept, whereas "instead of" excludes. That's arguably a wrong statement (the words say keep that, not the other). Hmm. But the conjunction word "instead of" is on the coordination wire, so the exclusion is recorded. Does the schema allow "instead of" as conjunction? The coordination wire has `conjunction`. Grammar-wise "instead of" is a preposition, not a conjunction. L3 lists "A relation has ... a `marker` that is no linking word" for relations; for coordination: "A coordination has a wrong conjunct".

Alternatively, the acceptable reading: relation marked "instead of" from c2 to n4. The sop chose coordination. Hmm. Is this a "wrong statement"? The nominal "the one we just discussed" — the relation r2 ties n4 to c3, so it's not lost.

Let me weigh: the judge's question: can the next layer continue, or must it undo a wrong statement? A coordination of "that" and "the one" with conjunction "instead of" — the conjunction word makes clear it's exclusion, not addition. I think this is a plausible encoding; the next layer isn't misled. But strictly, "instead of" is a preposition and a coordination of two nominals under it says they are put side by side...

Hmm, note in row 11 (n=37) the sop used relation marker "instead of" from c4 to c5 — proper. In row 20 it's a coordination. The rules don't explicitly cover "preposition used as conjunction". The closest: L3 "A coordination has a wrong conjunct" — are n3 and n4 wrong conjuncts? Under "instead of", "that" and "the one" are alternatives, not conjuncts. I'd call that L3: the coordination states the wrong relation between the two nominals.

Hmm, but is it "wrong" or just an encoding variance? The rules repeatedly forgive structural choices where grammar allows several. Grammar does not allow "instead of" as a coordinating conjunction. So the coordination is not a grammar-allowed reading. But the wire's conjunction field holds "instead of", so semantics are preserved...

Compare with settled case: "A coordination with what the verb acts on states a second thing acted on: L3" — that's about the time phrase case. The spirit: a coordination asserts both things are acted on. Here a coordination of "that" and "the one" as complement of "keep" states both are kept, which contradicts "instead of". Though the conjunction word carries the correction...

I think a fair reading: the conjunction word "instead of" is not a conjunction; the coordination thus mis-states the tie. I'll grade L3. Correction: use relation marker "instead of" from c2 to n4.

Hmm, but wait, careful: the note must quote words and name the wrong statement. "'instead of the one we just discussed' is written as a coordination of 'that' and 'the one', which states both are kept; the words say one replaces the other."

Hmm, but is this overly strict? Risk either way. Let me consider the grading distribution intent: the sop and alt differ; the "advanced" set = spaCy and hmm-rules disagree. Both formalizers are LLM outputs probably. The judge grades sop only. Being too lenient = all L8; too strict = many rejections. The rules say "Judge fairly: a plausible or incomplete reading that the next layer can continue from is acceptable; reject only a wrong statement or lost explicit information."

A coordination labelled with conjunction "instead of" — I'd say the next layer reads "keep that, instead of the one" and continues. It's not misled. Hmm. But the coordination wire's meaning is "wires put side by side" with conjunction; with conjunction "instead of" the meaning is clear.

I'll go L8 for n=54, to stay fair. Hmm, but then what about the nominal "the one we just discussed" tied to c3 — fine.

Hmm, hold on. Also check: k2 is used as c2's complement (complement=$k2). Does the schema allow a coordination as complement? "complement holds the nominals the verb takes" — a coordination of nominals as complement; plausible.

Decision: L8.

Row 21 (n=55): "I'd prefer the male option, and give the avatar a hat now."
SOP: c1 declarative aux "'d" verb prefer; k1 "and" c1 c2; c2 declarative verb give modifier "now" complement n3 n4. Hmm — "give the avatar a hat now" is a command; written as declarative without subject. Per settled case: "a verb after 'and' or 'then' that follows a clause with a `subject` and an `auxiliary`, in the form that auxiliary takes, may share them: a clause with no subject of its own, declarative or nonfinite." Here c1 has subject "I" and auxiliary "'d" (= would). "give" is not in the form "would" takes (bare infinitive) — actually "give" IS the bare form after "would": "I'd prefer ... and give ...". Hmm, "I'd prefer the male option, and give the avatar a hat now" — with "I'd" the reading "and [I'd] give" is grammatical and is exactly the settled case: verb after "and" following a clause with subject and auxiliary, in the form that auxiliary takes → may share them, clause with no subject of its own, declarative. "give" is the form "would" takes. So declarative is allowed by that settled case. Also lowering as imperative passes too. L8.

Row 22 (n=56): "Make my avatar a man character, then put a scarf on the avatar." L8 (as seen). Check n2 "a man character" head character, dep a, man. Fine.

Row 29 (n=87): L8. Row 30 (n=90): L8. Row 31 (n=91): L8 (same pattern as n=74). Row 32 (n=95): L8.

Row 33 (n=97): same as n=32 sop. L8.

Row 34 (n=98): "I want my avatar to be a female figure for every session from now on, not only for the diagram I have open right now."
SOP: k1 coordination conjunction "not only" conjunct=$r2 conjunct=$r4 — a coordination of two relations (r2 "for every session" and r4 "for the diagram..."). Is that allowed? The schema: coordination joins wires; conjunct can be relations? "wires put side by side" — yes, relations can be coordinated. And "not only ... " implies "but also" elided; here "not only for X" — hmm, the coordination with conjunction "not only" joining the two "for" relations makes sense: "for every session ... not only for the diagram ...". The word "not" is in the conjunction field of the coordination. Hmm — is "not" a negation word held in a coordination's conjunction? L1 says "An auxiliary or negation word is held in another place, or negates the wrong clause." Here "not" is in the conjunction of a coordination joining the two relations, which negates the second relation being exclusive... Actually "not only X" is a focus construction.

Compare with row 8 (n=33) where "not" was in discourse → L2. Here it's in a conjunction marker of a coordination whose conjuncts are the two "for" phrases — the meaning "not only for the diagram" is preserved: the coordination between r2 and r4 with "not only" says the second doesn't replace the first. I think it's a plausible encoding and the negation is not lost. L8.

Hmm, but strictly, "for" is in r4 too and "not" is a negation word not in a `negation` key. L1's clause: "An `auxiliary` or `negation` word is held in another place, or negates the wrong clause." Where is "not" held? In the conjunction of a coordination. Which is "another place" than `negation`. But it clearly marks r4's negation. Hmm, this is a judgement call. The coordination is between the relations themselves, and it says "not only r4". Would the next layer be misled? No — it reads that the "for the diagram" phrase doesn't limit the statement.

I'll pass L8.
